tb-E103-1.question:
Which of the following statements must be correct?

(1) The parallax of a nearby star is larger than that of a more distant star.

(2) The larger the parallax, the larger the angular shift of a star.

(3) If the distance to a star is 1 pc, the maximum angular shift of a star over six months is 1″.

A (1) only

B (3) only

C (1) and (2) only

D (1) and (3) only
tb-E103-1.reasoning:
By p = 1d, the closer the star to us, the larger its parallax is.

∴ (1) is correct.

Maximum angular shift is twice the parallax.

∴ (2) is correct.

By p = 1d, p = 1".

Maximum angular shift is twice the parallax and so it should be 2".

∴ (3) is incorrect.

source.name: E103 Revision 3 Stars and the Universe.docx

tb-E103-4.question:
What happens to the blackbody radiation curve of a star if it is moving towards the Earth?

A It has no change at all.

B It peaks at a lower intensity.

C It peaks at a longer wavelength.

D It peaks at a shorter wavelength.
tb-E103-4.reasoning:
When the star is moving towards the Earth, the whole spectrum of the star is blue-shifted. Therefore, its blackbody radiation curve should peak at a shorter wavelength and with higher intensity.

∴ A, B and C are incorrect.

tb-E103-5.question: Which of the following sets of curves show(s) the blackbody radiation curves of the same blackbody at different surface temperatures?
tb-E103-5.reasoning:
Blackbody radiation curves do not intersect with each other.

∴ B is incorrect.

The curve at a lower temperature has lower intensity at all wavelengths and peaks at a longer wavelength.

∴ C and D are incorrect.

tb-E103-6.question:
As observed from the Earth, the positions of Venus, Jupiter and the Moon on a particular day are shown in Figure a. They almost form an equilateral triangle in the sky.

Which of the following statements about the three celestial bodies must be correct?

(1) The angular distances between any two of them are roughly equal.

(2) The distances between any two of them are roughly equal.

(3) Their angular diameters are roughly equal.

A (1) only

B (1) and (2) only

C (2) and (3) only

D (1), (2) and (3)
tb-E103-6.reasoning:
Angular distance describes the apparent distance between two objects in the sky.

∴ (1) is correct.

Angular measurements do not represent actual distances of the celestial bodies.

∴ (2) is incorrect.

The Moon has a larger angular diameter than Jupiter and Venus.

∴ (3) is incorrect.

tb-E103-7.question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct?

(1) A blackbody at 2380 K emits roughly twice as much radiation per unit surface area as the same blackbody at 2000 K.

(2) The power radiated per unit surface area of a blackbody is determined solely by its surface temperature.

(3) The surface temperature of a blackbody determines its colour.

A (1) only

B (1) and (3) only

C (2) and (3) only

D (1), (2) and (3)
tb-E103-7.reasoning:
By Stefan’s law, J = σT4.

⇒ J1J2 = (T1T2)4 = (23802000)4 = 2.01 ≈ 2

J depends on T only.

∴ (1) and (2) are correct.

The intensity of radiation emitted by a blackbody depends only on its surface temperature. The relative intensity of visible light determines the colour of the blackbody.

∴ (3) is correct.

source.name: E103 Revision 3 Stars and the Universe.docx

tb-E103-12.question:
Compared with the Sun, Star X gives out more radiation per unit surface area at every wavelength. However, the Sun is more luminous. Which of the following descriptions about star X is correct?

A Star X is larger than the Sun.

B Star X is a red giant star.

C Star X is bluer than the Sun.

D Star X has a lower surface temperature than the Sun.
tb-E103-12.reasoning:
Since X gives out more radiation per unit surface area at every wavelength, it must have a higher temperature than the Sun.

∴ D is incorrect.

X is less luminous than the Sun even its surface temperature is higher. This means that X is smaller than the Sun.

∴ A is incorrect.

A red giant should have lower temperature than the Sun but with higher luminosity.

∴ B is incorrect.

The radiation emitted by X should peak at a shorter wavelength. Therefore, X should look bluer.

∴ C is correct.

Jimmy took two photographs of star P, one in January and one in March. Figure f shows the positions of the Earth in these two months. Jimmy tries to use the photographs to determine the distance of P from the Earth.

distance of the star < 10.15″2 = 13.3 pc

tb-E103-23.question:
The wavelength of a spectral line from iron is 525 nm. In the spectrum of star P, the same spectral line appears as 525.17 nm. It is known that star P orbits a very massive star in a circular orbit.

(a) At what radial velocity is star P moving with respect to us? (2 marks)

(b) Would star P appear to be hotter or cooler than it actually is? Explain your answer. (2 marks)
tb-E103-23.answer:
(a) ∆λ = 525.17 − 525 = 0.17 nm

By ∆λλ0 ≈ vrc,

radial velocity

≈ (∆λλ0)c

= (0.17525) × 3.00 × 108 1M

= 9.71 × 104 m s−1 (away from the Earth) 1A

(b) The whole spectrum would shift to longer wavelengths compared with that when it is at rest. 1A

The star appears to emit radiation with longer wavelengths, so it would appear to be cooler. 1A

tb-E103-24.question:
Stars X and Y have equal absolute magnitude. The intensity of Y is 10 000 times that of X as observed from the Earth.

(a) Calculate the ratio of the distance of star X to that of star Y from the Earth. (2 marks)

(b) Star Y has a stellar parallax of 0.08″. What is the stellar parallax of star X? (2 marks)

(c) Calculate the distances of stars X and Y from the Earth. (3 marks)

(d) The surface temperature of star X is 9 times that of Y. What is the ratio of their radius? Explain your answer. (3 marks)

(e) Star X is class B star. What type of star is Y? (1 mark)
tb-E103-24.answer:
(a) By b = L4πd2,

dXdY = bYbX

= 10 000 1M

= 100 1A

∴ dX : dY = 100 : 1

(b) By d = 1p,

pXpY = dYdX

⇒ pX = dYdX × pY

= 1100 × 0.08" 1M

= 0.0008" 1A

(c) By d = 1p,

Distance of star Y =1p

= 10.08 1M

= 12.5 pc 1A

Distance of star X = 12.5 × 100

= 1250 pc 1A

(d) By L = 4πR2σT4,

RXRY = TY4TX4

= 194 1M

= 181

∴ RX : RY = 1 : 81 1A

As X and Y have equal absolute magnitude, they have the same luminosity. Therefore, Y with a lower surface temperature has a larger radius.

1A

(e) Class M. 1A

The surface temperature of Y is one-ninth that of X. The surface temperature of a class B star ranges from 10 000 K to 25 000 K. Therefore, the surface temperature of Y should range from 1110 K to 2780 K which belongs to class M.

tb-E103-25.question:
Figure l shows a plot of apparent magnitude m against absolute magnitude M. The slope of the dotted line is 1. Y and Z are two stars.

(a) What are the distances to the stars that lie on the dotted line? Explain your answer. (2 marks)

(b) Explain whether the distance to Z is larger or smaller than the distance mentioned in (a). (2 marks)

(c) Hence, compare the distances to Y and Z. (1 mark)
tb-E103-25.answer:
(a) Since the slope of the dotted line is 1, for the stars lying on the dotted line, m = M. 1A

Hence, they are 10 pc away from the Earth. 1A

(b) The apparent magnitude of Z is larger than its absolute magnitude.

This means that the star would look brighter if it was 10 pc away from the Earth. 1A

Therefore, the distance to Z is larger than 10 pc. 1A

(c) Following the argument in (b), we can conclude that Y is within 10 pc from the Earth,

so the distance to Y is smaller than that to Z. 1A

source.name: E103 Revision 3 Stars and the Universe.docx

tb-E103-27.question:
Some dark lines are observed on the radiation spectra of a source on Earth and from a distant star (Fig m).

(a) What kind of spectra are shown in Figure m? (1 mark)

(b) Explain briefly how the dark lines are formed. (2 marks)

(c) Explain why the position of the lines is different in the two spectra. (2 marks)

(d) What is the relationship between the radial velocity of the star and the positions of the dark lines? (2 marks)
tb-E103-27.answer:
(a) Absorption spectra 1A

tb-E103-28.question:
(a) Hubble’s law can be mathematically presented as v = Hd, where H is a proportionality constant called Hubble constant. What do v and d represent? (2 marks)

(b) Figure n shows a graph of fractional shifts of wavelength (Δλλ0) of distant galaxies against d.

(i) Express the slope of the graph in terms of H and c. (2 marks)

(ii) The spectrum of a galaxy contains a line with wavelength 659.6 nm. When measured in a laboratory, this line from a stationary source has a wavelength of 656.3 nm. Find the distance of the galaxy from the Earth in Mpc. Take H = 73 km s–1 Mpc–1. (2 marks)
tb-E103-28.answer:
(a) v represents the receding velocity of a galaxy. 1A

d represents the distance to the galaxy from the Earth. 1A

(b) (i) By v = Hd and Δλλ0 ≈ vrc,

Δλλ0c ≈ Hd 1M

Δλλ0 ≈ (Hc)d

∴ Slope of the graph ≈ Hc 1A

(ii) From the result of (b)(i),

d ≈ (cH)(Δλλ0)

= (3.00 × 10873 × 103)(659.6 - 656.3656.3) 1M

= 20.7 Mpc 1A

source.name: E103 Revision 3 Stars and the Universe.docx

tb-E103-29.question:
David observes the spectrum of a galaxy X. He then plots a graph of the observed wavelengths of galaxy X against that observed from a stationary source (Fig o).

(a) Explain the physical meaning of the slope when its value is (i) larger than 1, (ii) equal to 1 and (iii) smaller than 1. (3 marks)

(b) Suppose the value of the slope is 1.001. Calculate the radial velocity of galaxy X. (3 marks)

(c) State an assumption you made in (b). (1 mark)
tb-E103-29.answer:
(a) (i) A slope larger than 1 represents a red shift, i.e. the galaxy is receding from the Earth. 1A

(ii) A slope equal to 1 represents neither a red shift or a blue shift, i.e. the distance between the galaxy and the Earth remains constant / the radial velocity is zero. 1A

(iii) A slope smaller than 1 represents a blue shift, i.e. the galaxy is approaching the Earth. 1A

(b) The equation of the straight line is
λ = 1.001λ0. 1M

By Δλλ0 ≈ vrc,

vr ≈ (∆λλ0)c = (1.001λ0 - λ0λ0)c 1M

= 0.001 × 3.00 × 108

= 3.00 × 105 m s−1 1A

(c) The radial speed of X is much smaller than the speed of light. 1A

source.name: E103 Revision 3 Stars and the Universe.docx
